title: Why Dominant Alleles Do Not Spread

scenes.tts: A dominant allele shows up in heterozygotes as well as in homozygotes. So why does it not spread, generation by generation, until almost everyone shows it? That was the question put to the mathematician G. H. Hardy in nineteen oh eight. His answer was no. It became the reference point for population genetics.
scenes.visual: Rows of people dots, blue showing the dominant trait, creeping up generation by generation toward all blue; a red cross lands on the trend
scenes.narration: A dominant allele shows up in heterozygotes as well as in homozygotes. So why does it not spread, generation by generation, until almost everyone shows it? That was the question put to the mathematician G. H. Hardy in nineteen oh eight. His answer was no. It became the reference point for population genetics.

scenes.tts: Picture every egg and sperm in a population thrown into one pool. The pool holds copies of two alleles, M and N. Call the fraction of copies that are M, p. Call the fraction that are N, q. With only two alleles, p plus q equals one. In a sample of one thousand people, counting copies gives p of zero point five four two five.
scenes.visual: A pool of blue M and yellow N dots; it sorts into a bar split p and q, labelled with the sample values
scenes.caption: In a sample of 1,000 people, counting copies gives p of 0.5425.
scenes.narration: In a sample of 1,000 people, counting copies gives p of 0.5425.

scenes.tts: Now make each new zygote by drawing one egg and one sperm at random. The chance of drawing M from both is p times p. A heterozygote can arise two ways. M from the egg and N from the sperm has chance p q. The reverse has chance q p. These are the Hardy-Weinberg proportions. M M is p squared, M N is two p q, and N N is q squared.
scenes.visual: The p and q bar is laid along two sides of a square; the four cells fill in as areas; the two heterozygote cells merge
scenes.caption: Now make each new zygote by drawing one egg and one sperm at random. The chance of drawing M from both is p x p. A heterozygote can arise two ways. M from the egg and N from the sperm has chance pq. The reverse has chance qp. These are the Hardy-Weinberg proportions. MM is p², MN is 2pq, and NN is q².
scenes.narration: Now make each new zygote by drawing one egg and one sperm at random. The chance of drawing M from both is p x p. A heterozygote can arise two ways. M from the egg and N from the sperm has chance pq. The reverse has chance qp. These are the Hardy-Weinberg proportions. MM is p², MN is 2pq, and NN is q².

scenes.tts: Now count the M copies in the next generation. Their fraction is p squared plus p q. That equals p times p plus q. Since p plus q is one, the answer is simply p. The allele frequency has not moved, and one round of random mating restores these proportions, whatever they were before.
scenes.visual: The M column of the square is highlighted; p squared plus p q becomes p; the new bar matches the old bar
scenes.caption: Now count the M copies in the next generation. Their fraction is p² + pq. That equals p(p + q). Since p + q is 1, the answer is simply p. The allele frequency has not moved, and one round of random mating restores these proportions, whatever they were before.
scenes.narration: Now count the M copies in the next generation. Their fraction is p² + pq. That equals p(p + q). Since p + q is 1, the answer is simply p. The allele frequency has not moved, and one round of random mating restores these proportions, whatever they were before.

scenes.tts: The population is large, mating is random at this locus, and there is no selection, mutation, migration or drift. Real populations break these assumptions. Hardy-Weinberg is a null model: the expectation to compare data against. In our sample, the observed counts sit close to the expected ones. The chi-square is zero point two two, far below the critical value of three point eight four. With one degree of freedom, that means no evidence of departure.
scenes.visual: Assumption chips tick in; they give way to observed against expected bars for MM, MN and NN, with the chi-square compared to its critical value

Hardy-Weinberg is a null model: the expectation to compare data against. In our sample, the observed counts sit close to the expected ones. The chi-square is 0.22, far below the critical value of 3.84. With one degree of freedom, that means no evidence of departure.

scenes.tts: Dominance describes how alleles act inside one person. It says nothing about how common they become. To change how common an allele is, something has to act on the population. Keep this rule. With nothing acting, allele frequencies stay put.
